questions.q: As defined in the lesson, what is prompt injection?
options: A slower-than-expected model response
Crafted text that causes a model to treat attacker content as a new instruction instead of data
A model running out of available memory
A billing error on an API account
questions.explain: The lesson defines prompt injection as text crafted so the model treats it as an instruction rather than content to process.

questions.q: What distinguishes indirect prompt injection from direct prompt injection?
options: Indirect injection only works on open-source models
Indirect injection requires physical access to the server
In indirect injection, the malicious instruction is planted in content the AI reads on the user's behalf, not typed by the user
Indirect injection is a defense technique, not an attack
questions.explain: The lesson explains indirect injection as text planted somewhere the AI reads for the user, such as a webpage, rather than typed directly into the chat.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say there's no complete, clean fix for prompt injection?
options: Because there's no reliable syntactic boundary between instructions and data inside a prompt
Because no AI company has tried to address it
Because it only affects models released before 2023
Because it requires a hardware upgrade to fix
questions.explain: The lesson notes there's no built-in boundary comparable to SQL parameterization separating instructions from data in a prompt.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why does limiting a model's tools (least privilege) help against prompt injection?
options: It makes the model respond faster
It reduces hosting costs
It improves the model's writing style
If the model can't call a sensitive function in the first place, an injected instruction has nothing dangerous to trigger
questions.explain: The lesson lists least-privilege tools as a defense specifically because it removes the dangerous action an injection could otherwise trigger.

questions.q: In the lesson's hidden-text example, why would a human reviewer likely miss the injected instruction?
options: It was written in a foreign language
It was displayed as white text on a white background, blending into the page visually
It was encrypted with a password
It was placed in the page's HTML comments only
questions.explain: The lesson's example hides the injected instruction as white-on-white text, which a model still reads as plain text but a human skimming the page would not notice.
